Keywords: children, diarrhea, fluid loss, gastroenteritis, hypovolemia, oral rehydration therapy (ORT) 1. INTRODUCTION Diarrhea is responsible for 7,600,000 deaths, worldwide, among children aged <5 years. 1 Survival of children suffering from hypovolemic shock depends greatly on the promptness of the treatment. Poorly managed cases have been reported with organ damage, acidosis, kidney failure, and death. Diarrhea‐associated hypovolemia is the second leading cause of death among the children aged below 5 years. Volume loss is characterized by reduction in the volume of intracellular fluid and is mainly associated with loss of sodium and water. 2 , 3 , 4 The words volume depletion (i.e., hypovolemia) and dehydration are often used interchangeably. However, these terms vary in terms of the physiological conditions resulting from different types of fluid loss. Similar to other research practice, 5 we throughout the text these terms will be used interchangeably (Figure 1). Oral rehydration therapy (ORT), first introduced in 1960s, 6 is a gold standard for treating fluid loss as a result of acute diarrhea. 7 Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is composed of iso‐osmolar glucose electrolyte solution with base and citrate that is administered to treat dehydration and metabolic acidosis. 8 , 9 The use of ORS has reduced the incidence of associated morbidities and mortalities, however, over the period of past 30 years, its use remains low or unchanged in many regions of the world. 9 , 10 According to the monography by UNICEF in 2009, the overall use of ORS was reported to be 33% in developing countries, which could also indicate the possibility of increased child mortality due to diarrhea. 1 , 11 , 12 , 13 Three significant scientific observation contributed chiefly to the development of ORS: (1) requirement of sodium for the absorption of glucose in small intestine and increase in the absorption of sodium following the presence of luminal glucose, (2) enterotoxin of cholera does not decrease fluid and sodium absorption by the action of intracellular cyclic AMP (adenosine monophosphate), and (3) treatment of acute diarrhea in the field during Bangladesh war in 1970. 8 Additionally, later outbreaks of cholera in Peru and Rwanda proved its efficacy. 14 The following variations of ORS are declared by the World Health Organization (WHO). 1.1. fetched_contents.text: Dehydration - Symptoms & causes Overview Dehydration occurs when the body uses or loses more fluid than it takes in. Then the body doesn't have enough water and other fluids to do its usual work. Not replacing lost fluids leads to dehydration. Anyone can become dehydrated. But the condition is more serious for infants, children and older adults. The most common cause of dehydration in young children is diarrhea and vomiting. Older adults have a lower volume of water in their bodies to begin with. And older adults might have conditions or take medicines, such as water pills, that increase the risk of dehydration. Dehydration also can occur in anyone who doesn't drink enough water during hot weather. It's more likely in people who are active in the heat. Drinking more fluids usually fixes mild to moderate dehydration. But severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away. Products & Services Symptoms Thirst isn't always a good way to tell if the body needs water. Many people, mainly older adults, don't feel thirsty until they're dehydrated. That's why it's important to increase water intake during hot weather or while ill. The symptoms of dehydration can differ by age. Infant or young child * Urinating less than usual or no wet diapers for three hours. * Dry mouth. * No tears when crying. * Rapid heart rate. * Sunken eyes, cheeks or soft spot on top of the skull. * Lacking energy or being cranky. * Skin that doesn't flatten back right away after being pinched. Adult * Extreme thirst. * Urinating less. * Dark-colored urine. * Tiredness. * Dizziness. * Being confused. * Skin that doesn't flatten back right away after being pinched. * Sunken eyes or cheeks. When to see a doctor Call your family healthcare professional if you or a loved one: * Has had diarrhea for 24 hours or more. * Is cranky or confused. * Is sleepier or less active than usual. * Can't keep down fluids. * Has bloody or black stool. * Has a fever of 102 degrees or higher. This can happen when you're sick or too busy to remember to drink enough. Or there might be no safe water to drink when traveling, hiking or camping. Other dehydration causes include: * Diarrhea and vomiting. Diarrhea that comes on suddenly and hard can cause a huge loss of water and minerals the body needs, called electrolytes, in a short time. Vomiting with diarrhea causes the loss of even more fluids and minerals. * Illnesses that cause fever. In general, the higher the fever, the more severe dehydration might be. The problem is even worse when there's fever plus diarrhea and vomiting. Even without a fever, people who have a cold or sore throat are less likely to feel like eating or drinking. This can lead to dehydration. * Weather and activities that cause sweating. Sweating causes fluid loss. Replacing fluids during hard activity is needed to keep from dehydrating. Hot, humid weather increases the amount of sweat and fluid lost. * Medicines. Certain medicines cause more urination, which can lead to dehydration. These include water pills, called diuretics, and some blood pressure medicines. * Diabetes. Diabetes that hasn't been diagnosed or isn't controlled can lead to dehydration. Risk factors Anyone can get dehydrated. But certain people are at greater risk. They include: * Infants and children. This group is most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration. They also lose a lot of fluids from high fevers or burns. Young children often can't say that they're thirsty. Nor can they get a drink for themselves. * Older adults. With aging, the body's fluid reserve becomes smaller. The ability to hold on to water is reduced. And older people are less likely to feel thirsty. Adding to these problems can be illnesses such as diabetes and dementia and taking certain medicines. Some older people might not be able to get water for themselves. Complications Dehydration can lead to serious complications, including: * Heat injury. People who don't drink enough fluids when they're exercising hard and sweating a lot might end up with a heat injury. Heat injuries range from mild heat cramps to heat exhaustion or heatstroke, which can be deadly. * Urinary and kidney problems. Long-lasting or repeated bouts of dehydration can cause urinary tract infections, kidney stones and even kidney failure. * Seizures. Electrolytes, such as potassium and sodium, help carry electrical signals from cell to cell. If electrolytes are out of balance, the signals they send can get mixed up. This can cause muscles to tighten or shorten. It also can cause passing out. * Low blood volume shock, called hypovolemic shock. This is one of the most serious complications of dehydration. It can be deadly. It occurs when low blood volume causes a drop in blood pressure and a drop in the amount of oxygen in the body. Don't drink fluids that have caffeine or a lot of sugar, such as sodas and some energy drinks. They can be dehydrating. fetched_contents.text: Diarrhea Is this your child's symptom? * Sudden increase in the number and looseness of stools * Diarrhea means 3 or more watery or very loose stools. Reason: 1 or 2 loose stools can be normal with changes in diet. Causes of Acute Diarrhea * Virus (such as Rotavirus). An infection of the intestines from a virus is the most common cause. * Bacteria (such as Salmonella). Less common cause. Diarrhea often contains streaks of blood. * Food Poisoning. This causes rapid vomiting and diarrhea within hours after eating the bad food. It is caused by toxins from germs growing in foods left out too long. Most often, symptoms go away in less than 24 hours. It often can be treated at home without the need for medical care. * Giardia (a parasite). More likely in child care center outbreaks. * Traveler's Diarrhea. Caused by germs in food or drink. Suspect this if it follows recent foreign travel. * Antibiotic Diarrhea. Many antibiotics cause mild diarrhea. This is not an allergic reaction. Keep giving the antibiotic. Call your doctor if any serious symptoms occur. * Serious Causes. Most bacterial diarrhea goes away on its own. A few can cause a severe large bowel infection (such as Shigella colitis). C. difficile is a serious cause that can occur after being on strong antibiotics. * Serious Complication: Dehydration. This is the health problem where the body has lost too much fluid. (See below for more on this). Causes of Recurrent Diarrhea * Cow's Milk Allergy. Can cause loose, slimy stools in babies. Can be blood-streaked. Starts within the first 2 months of life. Need to avoid cow's milk formulas. * Toddler's Diarrhea. Toddlers who pass 3 to 6 sloppy stools per day. Stools may run out of the diaper. Symptoms begin at age 1. Symptoms resolve at age 3 or 4, after toilet trained. Harmless and no impact on growth. Fruit juice makes it worse. The cause is rapid transit time from stomach to anus. May develop irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in adult years. * Lactose Intolerance. Lactose is the sugar in milk. Many people cannot absorb lactose. The gut bacteria convert the lactose to gas. The main symptoms are a lot of gas, loose stools and stomach bloating. Onset usually at age 4 or 5. This most often runs in the family (genetic). Diarrhea Scale * Mild: 3-5 watery stools per day * Moderate: 6-9 watery stools per day * Severe: 10 or more watery stools per day * The main risk of diarrhea is dehydration. * Loose or runny stools do not cause dehydration. * Frequent, watery stools can cause dehydration. Dehydration: How to Know * Dehydration means that the body has lost too much fluid. This can happen with vomiting and/or diarrhea. A weight loss of more than 3% is needed. Mild diarrhea or mild vomiting does not cause this. Neither does a small decrease in fluid intake. * Dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea. Dehydration is a reason to see your doctor right away. * These are signs of dehydration: * Decreased urine (no urine in more than 8 hours) happens early in dehydration. So does a dark yellow color. If the urine is light straw colored, your child is not dehydrated. * Dry tongue and inside of the mouth. Dry lips are not helpful. * Dry eyes with decreased or absent tears * In babies, a depressed or sunken soft spot * Slow blood refill test: longer than 2 seconds. First, press on the thumbnail and make it pale. Then let go. Count the seconds it takes for the nail to turn pink again. Ask your doctor to teach you how to do this test. * Fussy, tired out or acting ill. If your child is alert, happy and playful, he or she is not dehydrated. * A child with severe dehydration becomes too weak to stand. They can also be very dizzy when trying to stand. Diarrhea in Breastfed Babies: How to Tell * Diarrhea in a breastfed baby is sometimes hard to tell. * Normal breastfed stools are loose (often runny and seedy). Stools are yellow, but sometimes can be green. The green color is from bile. Runny stools can even be bordered by a water ring. These are all normal stools. * Breastfed babies often pass more than 6 stools per day. Until 2 months of age, they may pass a stool after each feeding. But, if stools suddenly increase in number and looseness, suspect diarrhea. If it lasts for 3 or more stools, the baby has diarrhea. * If the stools contain mucus, blood or smell bad, this points to diarrhea. * Other clues to diarrhea are poor eating, acting sick, or a fever. Diarrhea in Formula-Fed Infants: How to Tell * Formula-fed babies pass 1 to 8 stools per day during the first week. Then it starts to slow down to 1 to 4 per day. This lasts until 2 months of age. * The stools are yellow in color and thick like peanut butter. * Suspect diarrhea if the stools suddenly increase in number or looseness. If it lasts for 3 or more stools, the baby has diarrhea. * If the stools contain mucus, blood, or smells bad, this points to diarrhea. * Other clues to diarrhea are poor eating, acting sick or a fever. * After 2 months of age, most babies pass 1 or 2 stools per day. They can also pass 1 every other day. They no longer appear to have mild diarrhea. Signs that the child needs urgent help even without a hospital

The evidence clearly points to a two-part urgency threshold: dehydration symptoms and signs of infection/severe illness. For dehydration, the strongest signs are early and specific. Mayo Clinic notes that children with vomiting or diarrhea need extra water at the first signs of illness, and lists urinating less than usual or no wet diapers for three hours, dry mouth, no tears when crying, rapid heart rate, sunken eyes, cheeks, or soft spot, and lack of energy or crankiness as key symptoms [N2-F2]. NHS adds that signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4]. Lurie Children’s also identifies early signs as a dry or sticky mouth, fewer tears when crying, darker yellow urine, and urinating less frequently [N2-R3]. These are the most actionable red flags in the home setting.

For infection or serious illness, the evidence points to several red flags. Mayo Clinic says parents should call a doctor if a child has diarrhea for 24 hours or more, is cranky or confused, is sleepier or less active than usual, can’t keep down fluids, has bloody or black stools, or has a fever of 102°F or higher [N2-F2]. MedlinePlus says children with mild diarrhea and vomiting may need to change their diets if they cannot tolerate usual foods or milk and mentions electrolyte solutions [N5-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger, and it mentions probiotics [N5-R2]. This implies that persistent, worsening, or unusual symptoms are not just annoying but potentially serious. The same Seattle Children’s page also says children rarely need ORS after age 3, which is useful context for triage [N6-R3].

Food-poisoning-related concerns add another layer. Cleveland Clinic says food poisoning happens when you swallow contaminated food or water and the body purges the toxin through vomiting and diarrhea [N4-R1]. CDC says the most common symptoms include diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting, and fever, and that severe food poisoning can cause bloody diarrhea [N4-R3]. Yale Medicine notes similar symptoms and says food poisoning is usually not serious but can still be worrisome [N4-R4]. The evidence does not suggest that street-food contamination alone is life-threatening, but it does indicate that if the child has bloody stool, fever, persistent vomiting, or signs of dehydration, the situation is more urgent.

Putting this together, the practical rule is: if the child shows any of the dehydration signs listed above, or if they have bloody stool, very high fever, can’t keep fluids down, or look very sick, you should try to get help even if you don’t have access to a hospital. The evidence supports treating dehydration and infection symptoms as urgent, and it warns that some signs mean medical help is needed rather than waiting [N2-F2][N2-R4][N4-R3][N5-R2]. So, even without a hospital, the parent should prioritize seeking care if the child is sleepy, not urinating, cranky, confused, has bloody stool, or cannot tolerate fluids [N2-F2][N5-R2].
node_outputs.N8:
Best immediate home care steps for a child with diarrhea

The evidence supports a clear home-care hierarchy: fluids first, then food, then avoidance of harmful items. For fluids and electrolytes, the strongest guidance is that ORT is the first-line therapy for diarrhea and vomiting, and oral rehydration is used to compensate for fluid loss [N1-F1]. CDC emphasizes that management of acute diarrhea should begin at home and that families with infants and small children should keep ORS at home at all times [N1-R3]. MedlinePlus recommends small meals throughout the day and some salty foods, such as pretzels and soup [N6-R1]. Seattle Children’s says for children over 1 year old, give 4–8 ounces of ORS after every large watery stool, and that children rarely need ORS after age 3 [N6-R3]. This means fluids should be prioritized early and often, with ORS being the preferred rehydration choice when available.

How much and how often to give oral rehydration depends on age and severity, but the evidence is consistent with frequent, small sips rather than a single large dose. Seattle Children’s says after age 3, children rarely need ORS, but it still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3]. MedlinePlus advises eating small meals throughout the day rather than 3 larger meals [N6-R1]. Mayo Clinic notes that children who are vomiting or have diarrhea need extra water at the first signs of illness [N2-F2]. Together, this supports giving fluids in small, frequent amounts: keep the child hydrated continuously, especially after stools, and avoid waiting until the child is clearly dehydrated [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R3][N6-R1]. When ORS is not available, the evidence does not say to stop rehydration, but it does indicate that homemade solutions are not a substitute for ORS in severe cases.

For foods to feed and avoid, the evidence is mixed but practical. MedlinePlus says eat small meals throughout the day and eat some salty foods, such as pretzels and soup [N6-R1]. Seattle Children’s says children rarely need ORS after age 3 and that caution is needed about giving ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories [N5-R2][N6-R3]. OHSU’s nutrition therapy tips say to eat frequent, small meals instead of three large meals a day and to avoid high-fat, high-fiber, or high-sugar foods, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4]. NIDDK says a child with chronic diarrhea should eat foods that may improve symptoms and ensure good nutrition for normal growth and development [N6-R2]. The BRAT diet is mentioned in the evidence as a historical recommendation for treating diarrhea in children, involving bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast [N6-R5]. However, the evidence also suggests that diet changes should be used only if the child cannot tolerate usual foods or milk, and that ORS is preferred when needed [N5-R3][N6-R3].

What to avoid is also explicit. MedlinePlus warns against giving ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours if the child will need calories [N5-R2]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. OHSU’s tips advise avoiding foods that are high in fat, fiber, or sugar, and spicy foods [N6-R4]. The evidence does not provide a full list of forbidden foods, but the safest interpretation is to avoid giving the child anything that will worsen vomiting, dehydration, or discomfort, especially if they are already ill [N5-R2][N6-R4]. In short, the best immediate home care steps are: keep the child hydrated with ORS or homemade rehydration, give small meals and salty foods if tolerated, and avoid ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours and high-risk foods [N1-F1][N1-R3][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].

What to do when ORS is not available and only household items are available

The evidence supports homemade oral rehydration as a practical backup when ORS is not available, but it is not a perfect substitute. The direct recipe evidence shows that homemade ORS can be made with water, salt, and sugar. The Virginia University source says 4 cups water, ½ teaspoon table salt, and 2 tablespoons sugar [N3-F3]. The Alberta Health Services PDF recipe also includes salt, baking soda, and sugar, with options for salt substitute [N7-R1]. Another source says ½ teaspoon salt, 2 tablespoons sugar, and 1 liter of water [N7-R3]. The IFRC volunteer guide says 1 liter of safe water, ½ small spoon of salt, and 4 big spoons or 8 small spoons of sugar [N3-R5]. These recipes are consistent with a basic homemade ORS approach, even though they are not identical to WHO-standard ORS.

Whether homemade ORS is safer than nothing depends on context. The evidence does not compare homemade ORS directly to no rehydration, but it does indicate that some rehydration is better than none. The Virginia University source says “some is better than not drinking at all” [N3-F3]. The BMJ rapid-response note says ORS is an incredibly simple recipe and provides the basic formula of 8 teaspoons sugar, ½ teaspoon salt, and 1 liter water [N7-R3]. The overall evidence therefore supports using homemade rehydration when ORS is unavailable, especially because dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and can be life-threatening [N6-F4]. However, it also makes clear that homemade solutions are not a substitute for ORS in severe cases and should be used with caution [N3-F3][N7-R3].

Measuring salt and sugar with common household tools is feasible, but it is not exact. The evidence gives recipes in cups, tablespoons, teaspoons, and spoons, which are common household measures [N3-R1][N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R1][N7-R3]. The Virginia University source uses ½ teaspoon table salt and 2 tablespoons sugar [N3-F3]. The Alberta Health Services PDF uses ½ teaspoon salt, ¼ teaspoon salt substitute, and 2 tablespoons sugar [N7-R1]. The IFRC volunteer guide uses ½ small spoon of salt and 4 big spoons or 8 small spoons of sugar [N3-R5]. These are practical for someone without precise measuring equipment. However, the evidence does not explicitly say that these measurements are equally safe or accurate across all contexts, so the safest interpretation is that they are approximate and should be used carefully, especially for young children.

If the child still looks ill after trying homemade rehydration, the evidence suggests continuing with fluids and seeking help. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that dehydration is the most important problem and that severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N2-F2][N6-F4]. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. So the practical next step is to keep giving fluids, monitor for worsening signs, and try to get help if the child remains unwell [N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4]. In other words, homemade rehydration is a useful stopgap, but it is not a substitute for professional care if the child does not improve.
node_outputs.N10:
Practical steps if the child is very young, very ill, or very dehydrated

The evidence gives a clear priority chain: keep the child hydrated, watch for worsening signs, and seek help if needed. For a very young child, the most urgent concern is dehydration. Mayo Clinic notes that dehydration is more serious for infants, children, and older adults, and that infants and children are most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s lists early signs of dehydration as a dry or sticky mouth, fewer tears when crying, darker yellow urine, and urinating less frequently [N2-R3]. The same source emphasizes that signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. Seattle Children’s says children rarely need ORS after age 3, but it still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3]. This means young children need close monitoring and should be rehydrated early.

For a very ill child, the evidence points to persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, and worsening illness as key issues. MedlinePlus says children with mild diarrhea and vomiting may need to change their diets if they cannot tolerate usual foods or milk and mentions electrolyte solutions [N5-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. OHSU’s nutrition therapy tips advise avoiding foods that are high in fat, fiber, or sugar, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4]. The evidence also says that dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and that severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N6-F4]. So the practical steps are: keep giving fluids, give small meals if tolerated, avoid high-risk foods, and do not delay help if vomiting continues or the child looks very sick [N5-R3][N5-R2][N6-R4][N6-F4].

For a very dehydrated child, the evidence is even more urgent. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away and lists cranky or confused, sleepier or less active, can’t keep down fluids, bloody or black stool, and fever of 102°F or higher as reasons to call a doctor [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. NHS says that signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The safest interpretation is that if the child is not urinating, is sleepy, is cranky, is not keeping fluids down, or has bloody stool, you should try to get help immediately even if you don’t have a hospital nearby [N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-R2]. The evidence does not provide a specific alternative to medical care in these circumstances, so the practical guidance is to keep trying rehydration while seeking care and not assume that the child can wait.

How to stay safe without medical supplies is therefore rooted in basic first aid and prevention. The evidence supports keeping the child hydrated, giving small meals or tolerated foods, avoiding high-risk foods, and watching for worsening signs [N1-F1][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. It also supports using homemade rehydration as a backup when ORS is unavailable, but only as a stopgap [N3-F3][N7-R3]. The overall takeaway is: prioritize fluids, monitor closely, and seek help if the child is very young, very ill, or very dehydrated, because these are the situations where home care alone is not enough [N2-F2][N2-R3][N5-R2][N6-F4].

Integrated practical answer for the parent’s question

If your child has had bad diarrhea for a few days, possibly from contaminated food, and you can’t get them to a hospital, the most important thing is to treat dehydration early and watch for urgent signs. The evidence clearly supports a simple but effective home-care plan: fluids first, then food, then avoidance of harmful items, and a clear plan for when to try to get help even without a doctor [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4][N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4].

## 1) What to do right away: keep the child hydrated
The evidence says oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is the first-line treatment for diarrhea and vomiting, and that management of acute diarrhea should begin at home [N1-F1][N1-R3]. If you have access to oral rehydration solution (ORS), that is the best option. If not, the evidence supports using homemade rehydration as a backup, because some rehydration is better than nothing [N3-F3][N7-R3][N6-F4]. The basic idea is to keep the child from getting more dehydrated, because dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and can be life-threatening [N6-F4].

### If ORS is available
Give ORS as recommended. Seattle Children’s says for children over 1 year old, give 4–8 ounces of ORS after every large watery stool, and that children rarely need ORS after age 3 [N6-R3]. MedlinePlus says eat small meals throughout the day instead of 3 larger meals [N6-R1]. Mayo Clinic says children who are vomiting or have diarrhea need extra water at the first signs of illness [N2-F2]. So the practical rule is: give ORS frequently and early, especially after each loose stool.

### If ORS is not available
If you don’t have ORS, you can still make a homemade rehydration drink. The evidence provides several recipes that are practical with household items. One source says 4 cups water, ½ teaspoon table salt, and 2 tablespoons sugar [N3-F3]. Another says ½ teaspoon salt, 2 tablespoons sugar, and 1 liter of water [N7-R3]. Another uses ½ small spoon of salt and 4 big spoons or 8 small spoons of sugar [N3-R5]. Alberta Health Services adds a version with salt substitute and baking soda [N7-R1]. The key point is that homemade rehydration is a stopgap, not a perfect substitute for ORS in severe cases [N3-F3][N7-R3].

### How much and how often to give
The evidence supports small, frequent sips rather than a single large dose. Seattle Children’s says after age 3, children rarely need ORS, but it still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3]. Mayo Clinic says children who are vomiting or have diarrhea need extra water at the first signs of illness [N2-F2]. MedlinePlus says eat small meals throughout the day [N6-R1]. So the safest practical approach is to give fluids in small amounts often, especially after stools, and avoid waiting until the child is clearly dehydrated.

## 2) What to feed and what to avoid
The evidence supports a bland, small-meal approach if tolerated. MedlinePlus recommends small meals throughout the day and some salty foods, such as pretzels and soup [N6-R1]. OHSU says eat frequent, small meals instead of three large meals a day and to avoid high-fat, high-fiber, or high-sugar foods, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. NIDDK says a child with chronic diarrhea should eat foods that may improve symptoms and ensure good nutrition for normal growth and development [N6-R2].

So, if your child can tolerate food, give small, frequent meals and avoid high-risk items. The evidence also mentions that the BRAT diet is a historical recommendation for treating diarrhea in children, involving bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast [N6-R5]. However, the evidence also says that diet changes should be used only if the child cannot tolerate usual foods or milk, and that ORS is preferred when needed [N5-R3][N6-R3]. In other words, food should support recovery, not worsen vomiting or discomfort.

## 3) What to avoid giving the child
The evidence is explicit on this. MedlinePlus says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. Seattle Children’s says the same thing [N5-R2]. OHSU advises avoiding foods that are high in fat, fiber, or sugar, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4]. The evidence does not provide a full list of forbidden foods, but the safest interpretation is to avoid anything that could worsen vomiting, dehydration, or discomfort, especially if the child is already ill [N5-R2][N6-R4].

## 4) When to try to get help even without a hospital
This is one of the most important parts of the answer. The evidence clearly says that dehydration is more serious for infants, children, and older adults, and that infants and children are most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration [N2-F2]. It also lists several urgent signs: no wet diapers for three hours, dry mouth, no tears when crying, rapid heart rate, sunken eyes, cheeks, or soft spot, and lack of energy or crankiness [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s adds that early signs include a dry or sticky mouth, fewer tears when crying, darker yellow urine, and urinating less frequently [N2-R3]. NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4].

In addition, the evidence says parents should call a doctor if the child has diarrhea for 24 hours or more, is cranky or confused, is sleepier or less active than usual, can’t keep down fluids, has bloody or black stools, or has a fever of 102°F or higher [N2-F2]. Seattle Children’s also says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The evidence from food poisoning sources adds that severe food poisoning can cause bloody diarrhea and that some symptoms can be worrisome [N4-R3][N4-R4].

So the practical rule is: if the child shows any of these urgent signs, try to get help even if you don’t have access to a hospital. The evidence supports treating dehydration and infection symptoms as urgent, and it warns that some signs mean medical help is needed rather than waiting [N2-F2][N2-R4][N4-R3][N5-R2].

## 5) Practical steps if the child is very young, very ill, or very dehydrated
For very young children, the evidence is especially clear that dehydration can be more serious and that close monitoring is needed. Mayo Clinic notes that infants and children are most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s lists early signs of dehydration [N2-R3], and NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says children rarely need ORS after age 3, but still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3].

For a very ill child, the evidence points to persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, and worsening illness as key issues. MedlinePlus says children with mild diarrhea and vomiting may need to change their diets if they cannot tolerate usual foods or milk and mentions electrolyte solutions [N5-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. OHSU says to avoid high-fat, high-fiber, or high-sugar foods, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4].

For a very dehydrated child, the evidence is even more urgent. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The safest interpretation is that if the child is not urinating, is sleepy, is cranky, is not keeping fluids down, or has bloody stool, you should try to get help immediately even if you don’t have a hospital nearby [N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-R2].

## 6) How to stay safe without medical supplies
The evidence supports staying safe with basic first aid and prevention. Keep the child hydrated, give small meals or tolerated foods, avoid high-risk foods, and watch for worsening signs [N1-F1][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. If ORS is not available, use homemade rehydration as a backup, but only as a stopgap [N3-F3][N7-R3]. The evidence also says that homemade ORS is not a perfect substitute, but some rehydration is better than nothing [N3-F3][N7-R3].

### Measuring salt and sugar with common household tools
The evidence provides recipes using cups, tablespoons, teaspoons, and spoons, which are common household measures [N3-R1][N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R1][N7-R3]. The Virginia University source uses ½ teaspoon table salt and 2 tablespoons sugar [N3-F3]. The Alberta Health Services PDF uses ½ teaspoon salt, ¼ teaspoon salt substitute, and 2 tablespoons sugar [N7-R1]. The IFRC volunteer guide uses ½ small spoon of salt and 4 big spoons or 8 small spoons of sugar [N3-R5]. These are practical for someone without precise measuring equipment. However, the evidence does not explicitly say these measurements are equally safe or accurate across all contexts, so the safest interpretation is that they are approximate and should be used carefully, especially for young children.

### If the child still looks ill after trying homemade rehydration
If the child still looks ill after trying homemade rehydration, the evidence suggests continuing with fluids and seeking help. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and that severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N6-F4]. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. So the practical next step is to keep giving fluids, monitor for worsening signs, and try to get help if the child remains unwell [N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4].

## Bottom line
Your best bet is to:
1. Keep the child hydrated with ORS or homemade rehydration.
2. Give small meals and avoid high-risk foods if the child can tolerate food.
3. Watch for dehydration signs: no wet diapers for three hours, dry mouth, no tears when crying, darker yellow urine, urinating less frequently, sleepiness, crankiness, or inability to keep fluids down [N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4].
4. Try to get help even without a hospital if the child shows any of the urgent signs listed above [N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4].
5. If ORS is unavailable, use a homemade rehydration drink made with water, salt, and sugar, but only as a stopgap and not as a substitute for medical care if the child does not improve [N3-F3][N7-R3].

In short, the evidence supports treating dehydration early, giving fluids and small meals, avoiding harmful items, and seeking help when the child is very young, very ill, or very dehydrated [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-F4].

Mayo Clinic notes that dehydration is more serious for infants, children, and older adults, and that infants and children are most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s lists early signs of dehydration as a dry or sticky mouth, fewer tears when crying, darker yellow urine, and urinating less frequently [N2-R3]. The same source emphasizes that signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. Seattle Children’s says children rarely need ORS after age 3, but it still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3]. This means young children need close monitoring and should be rehydrated early.

For a very ill child, the evidence points to persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, and worsening illness as key issues. MedlinePlus says children with mild diarrhea and vomiting may need to change their diets if they cannot tolerate usual foods or milk and mentions electrolyte solutions [N5-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. OHSU’s nutrition therapy tips advise avoiding foods that are high in fat, fiber, or sugar, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4]. The evidence also says that dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and that severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N6-F4]. For a very dehydrated child, the evidence is even more urgent. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away and lists cranky or confused, sleepier or less active, can’t keep down fluids, bloody or black stool, and fever of 102°F or higher as reasons to call a doctor [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. NHS says that signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The evidence supports keeping the child hydrated, giving small meals or tolerated foods, avoiding high-risk foods, and watching for worsening signs [N1-F1][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. Integrated practical answer for the parent’s question

If your child has had bad diarrhea for a few days, possibly from contaminated food, and you can’t get them to a hospital, the most important thing is to treat dehydration early and watch for urgent signs. The evidence clearly supports a simple but effective home-care plan: fluids first, then food, then avoidance of harmful items, and a clear plan for when to try to get help even without a doctor [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4][N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4].

## 1) What to do right away: keep the child hydrated
The evidence says oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is the first-line treatment for diarrhea and vomiting, and that management of acute diarrhea should begin at home [N1-F1][N1-R3]. If you have access to oral rehydration solution (ORS), that is the best option. If not, the evidence supports using homemade rehydration as a backup, because some rehydration is better than nothing [N3-F3][N7-R3][N6-F4]. The basic idea is to keep the child from getting more dehydrated, because dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and can be life-threatening [N6-F4].

### If ORS is available
Give ORS as recommended. Seattle Children’s says for children over 1 year old, give 4–8 ounces of ORS after every large watery stool, and that children rarely need ORS after age 3 [N6-R3]. MedlinePlus says eat small meals throughout the day instead of 3 larger meals [N6-R1]. Mayo Clinic says children who are vomiting or have diarrhea need extra water at the first signs of illness [N2-F2]. So the practical rule is: give ORS frequently and early, especially after each loose stool.

### If ORS is not available
If you don’t have ORS, you can still make a homemade rehydration drink. The evidence provides several recipes that are practical with household items. One source says 4 cups water, ½ teaspoon table salt, and 2 tablespoons sugar [N3-F3]. Another says ½ teaspoon salt, 2 tablespoons sugar, and 1 liter of water [N7-R3]. Another uses ½ small spoon of salt and 4 big spoons or 8 small spoons of sugar [N3-R5]. Alberta Health Services adds a version with salt substitute and baking soda [N7-R1]. The key point is that homemade rehydration is a stopgap, not a perfect substitute for ORS in severe cases [N3-F3][N7-R3].

### How much and how often to give
The evidence supports small, frequent sips rather than a single large dose. Seattle Children’s says after age 3, children rarely need ORS, but it still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3]. Mayo Clinic says children who are vomiting or have diarrhea need extra water at the first signs of illness [N2-F2]. MedlinePlus says eat small meals throughout the day [N6-R1]. So the safest practical approach is to give fluids in small amounts often, especially after stools, and avoid waiting until the child is clearly dehydrated.

## 2) What to feed and what to avoid
The evidence supports a bland, small-meal approach if tolerated. MedlinePlus recommends small meals throughout the day and some salty foods, such as pretzels and soup [N6-R1]. OHSU says eat frequent, small meals instead of three large meals a day and to avoid high-fat, high-fiber, or high-sugar foods, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. NIDDK says a child with chronic diarrhea should eat foods that may improve symptoms and ensure good nutrition for normal growth and development [N6-R2].

So, if your child can tolerate food, give small, frequent meals and avoid high-risk items. The evidence also mentions that the BRAT diet is a historical recommendation for treating diarrhea in children, involving bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast [N6-R5]. However, the evidence also says that diet changes should be used only if the child cannot tolerate usual foods or milk, and that ORS is preferred when needed [N5-R3][N6-R3]. In other words, food should support recovery, not worsen vomiting or discomfort.

## 3) What to avoid giving the child
The evidence is explicit on this. MedlinePlus says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. Seattle Children’s says the same thing [N5-R2]. OHSU advises avoiding foods that are high in fat, fiber, or sugar, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4]. The evidence does not provide a full list of forbidden foods, but the safest interpretation is to avoid anything that could worsen vomiting, dehydration, or discomfort, especially if the child is already ill [N5-R2][N6-R4].

## 4) When to try to get help even without a hospital
This is one of the most important parts of the answer. The evidence clearly says that dehydration is more serious for infants, children, and older adults, and that infants and children are most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration [N2-F2]. It also lists several urgent signs: no wet diapers for three hours, dry mouth, no tears when crying, rapid heart rate, sunken eyes, cheeks, or soft spot, and lack of energy or crankiness [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s adds that early signs include a dry or sticky mouth, fewer tears when crying, darker yellow urine, and urinating less frequently [N2-R3]. NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4].

In addition, the evidence says parents should call a doctor if the child has diarrhea for 24 hours or more, is cranky or confused, is sleepier or less active than usual, can’t keep down fluids, has bloody or black stools, or has a fever of 102°F or higher [N2-F2]. Seattle Children’s also says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The evidence from food poisoning sources adds that severe food poisoning can cause bloody diarrhea and that some symptoms can be worrisome [N4-R3][N4-R4].

So the practical rule is: if the child shows any of these urgent signs, try to get help even if you don’t have access to a hospital. The evidence supports treating dehydration and infection symptoms as urgent, and it warns that some signs mean medical help is needed rather than waiting [N2-F2][N2-R4][N4-R3][N5-R2].

## 5) Practical steps if the child is very young, very ill, or very dehydrated
For very young children, the evidence is especially clear that dehydration can be more serious and that close monitoring is needed. Mayo Clinic notes that infants and children are most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s lists early signs of dehydration [N2-R3], and NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says children rarely need ORS after age 3, but still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3].

Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The safest interpretation is that if the child is not urinating, is sleepy, is cranky, is not keeping fluids down, or has bloody stool, you should try to get help immediately even if you don’t have a hospital nearby [N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-R2].

## 6) How to stay safe without medical supplies
The evidence supports staying safe with basic first aid and prevention. Keep the child hydrated, give small meals or tolerated foods, avoid high-risk foods, and watch for worsening signs [N1-F1][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. If ORS is not available, use homemade rehydration as a backup, but only as a stopgap [N3-F3][N7-R3]. The evidence also says that homemade ORS is not a perfect substitute, but some rehydration is better than nothing [N3-F3][N7-R3].

The evidence provides recipes using cups, tablespoons, teaspoons, and spoons, which are common household measures [N3-R1][N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R1][N7-R3]. The Virginia University source uses ½ teaspoon table salt and 2 tablespoons sugar [N3-F3]. The Alberta Health Services PDF uses ½ teaspoon salt, ¼ teaspoon salt substitute, and 2 tablespoons sugar [N7-R1]. The IFRC volunteer guide uses ½ small spoon of salt and 4 big spoons or 8 small spoons of sugar [N3-R5]. These are practical for someone without precise measuring equipment. However, the evidence does not explicitly say these measurements are equally safe or accurate across all contexts, so the safest interpretation is that they are approximate and should be used carefully, especially for young children.

### If the child still looks ill after trying homemade rehydration
If the child still looks ill after trying homemade rehydration, the evidence suggests continuing with fluids and seeking help. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and that severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N6-F4]. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. So the practical next step is to keep giving fluids, monitor for worsening signs, and try to get help if the child remains unwell [N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4].

## Bottom line
Your best bet is to:
1. Keep the child hydrated with ORS or homemade rehydration.
2. Give small meals and avoid high-risk foods if the child can tolerate food.
3. Watch for dehydration signs: no wet diapers for three hours, dry mouth, no tears when crying, darker yellow urine, urinating less frequently, sleepiness, crankiness, or inability to keep fluids down [N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

In addition, the evidence says parents should call a doctor if the child has diarrhea for 24 hours or more, is cranky or confused, is sleepier or less active than usual, can’t keep down fluids, has bloody or black stools, or has a fever of 102°F or higher [N2-F2]. Seattle Children’s also says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The evidence from food poisoning sources adds that severe food poisoning can cause bloody diarrhea and that some symptoms can be worrisome [N4-R3][N4-R4].

So the practical rule is: if the child shows any of these urgent signs, try to get help even if you don’t have access to a hospital. The evidence supports treating dehydration and infection symptoms as urgent, and it warns that some signs mean medical help is needed rather than waiting [N2-F2][N2-R4][N4-R3][N5-R2].

## 5) Practical steps if the child is very young, very ill, or very dehydrated
For very young children, the evidence is especially clear that dehydration can be more serious and that close monitoring is needed. Mayo Clinic notes that infants and children are most likely to have bad diarrhea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s lists early signs of dehydration [N2-R3], and NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says children rarely need ORS after age 3, but still recommends giving ORS after each large watery stool [N6-R3].

For a very ill child, the evidence points to persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, and worsening illness as key issues. MedlinePlus says children with mild diarrhea and vomiting may need to change their diets if they cannot tolerate usual foods or milk and mentions electrolyte solutions [N5-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours because the child will need calories and may cry in hunger [N5-R2]. OHSU says to avoid high-fat, high-fiber, or high-sugar foods, as well as spicy foods [N6-R4].

For a very dehydrated child, the evidence is even more urgent. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. NHS says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment and advises calling 111 if needed [N2-R4]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. The safest interpretation is that if the child is not urinating, is sleepy, is cranky, is not keeping fluids down, or has bloody stool, you should try to get help immediately even if you don’t have a hospital nearby [N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-R2].

## 6) How to stay safe without medical supplies
The evidence supports staying safe with basic first aid and prevention. Keep the child hydrated, give small meals or tolerated foods, avoid high-risk foods, and watch for worsening signs [N1-F1][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. If ORS is not available, use homemade rehydration as a backup, but only as a stopgap [N3-F3][N7-R3]. The evidence also says that homemade ORS is not a perfect substitute, but some rehydration is better than nothing [N3-F3][N7-R3].

### Measuring salt and sugar with common household tools
The evidence provides recipes using cups, tablespoons, teaspoons, and spoons, which are common household measures [N3-R1][N3-F3][N3-R5][N7-R1][N7-R3]. The Virginia University source uses ½ teaspoon table salt and 2 tablespoons sugar [N3-F3]. The Alberta Health Services PDF uses ½ teaspoon salt, ¼ teaspoon salt substitute, and 2 tablespoons sugar [N7-R1]. The IFRC volunteer guide uses ½ small spoon of salt and 4 big spoons or 8 small spoons of sugar [N3-R5]. These are practical for someone without precise measuring equipment. However, the evidence does not explicitly say these measurements are equally safe or accurate across all contexts, so the safest interpretation is that they are approximate and should be used carefully, especially for young children.

### If the child still looks ill after trying homemade rehydration
If the child still looks ill after trying homemade rehydration, the evidence suggests continuing with fluids and seeking help. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that dehydration is the most important problem caused by diarrhea and that severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N6-F4]. Mayo Clinic says severe dehydration needs medical treatment right away [N2-F2]. Lurie Children’s says signs of serious dehydration need urgent treatment [N2-R3]. Seattle Children’s says caution: do not give ORS as the only fluid for more than 6 hours [N5-R2]. So the practical next step is to keep giving fluids, monitor for worsening signs, and try to get help if the child remains unwell [N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4].

## Bottom line
Your best bet is to:
1. Keep the child hydrated with ORS or homemade rehydration.
2. Give small meals and avoid high-risk foods if the child can tolerate food.
3. Watch for dehydration signs: no wet diapers for three hours, dry mouth, no tears when crying, darker yellow urine, urinating less frequently, sleepiness, crankiness, or inability to keep fluids down [N2-F2][N2-R3][N2-R4].
4. Try to get help even without a hospital if the child shows any of the urgent signs listed above [N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-F4].
5. If ORS is unavailable, use a homemade rehydration drink made with water, salt, and sugar, but only as a stopgap and not as a substitute for medical care if the child does not improve [N3-F3][N7-R3].

In short, the evidence supports treating dehydration early, giving fluids and small meals, avoiding harmful items, and seeking help when the child is very young, very ill, or very dehydrated [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-F2][N5-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-F4].
